opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Neha. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything or campaign for anyone. Nothing you tell me today will be linked to your name. I'll read you five short pictures of how AI might change things over the next five years, and ask how you'd react to each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'll warn you, I've got opinions. I was a UX copywriter, so I wrote the words in apps, the buttons and the error messages. My whole team got cut three months ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to people in your field, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the layoffs were never really about AI. Companies used it as cover to cut staff and please investors. I'd post that, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI really stays a tool, I'm fine. I'm good at what I do and I use these tools every day. I'd find a writing job in a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep up the course I'm doing in UX research, apply for content design roles, and take freelance work to stretch my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed more than scared. It would prove the cuts were greed, not progress.

S0.say: The layoffs were never really about AI; companies used it as cover to cut staff.
S0.think: If AI stays a tool, she's good enough to land a writing job within a few months.
S0.do: Keeps up her UX research course, applies for content design roles and freelances to stretch her savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it to people in your field, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about the junior jobs. If nobody hires beginners, where do the next senior people come from? It's short-term thinking dressed up as innovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not a beginner, so I'd probably squeeze in. But my kind of writing is exactly the task that disappears. I'd need to be the person who checks the AI's work, not the one who writes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the research course, build a portfolio showing I can test and fix AI-written text, and network hard. I'd give myself six months before taking anything that pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a path, but it's narrower than the one I trained for.

S1.say: If nobody hires beginners, where do the next senior people come from?
S1.think: She'd likely squeeze in, but only by checking AI's writing instead of doing the writing herself.
S1.do: Finishes her research course, builds a portfolio of testing and fixing AI-written text, and networks hard, with a six-month limit before taking any paid work.
S1.feel: Uneasy, the path is narrower than she trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it to people in your field, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. A few tech companies decided this. They should pay for it, through taxes, and workers should have a say before tools like this get rolled out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know what these tools can do because I use them. Routine writing is gone in this version. The new AI jobs exist, but there'd be a hundred of us for each one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply for those AI jobs anyway, testing and safety work. Move somewhere cheaper with a flatmate. And join a union or a campaign group, because I'd be furious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. Under the anger, pretty scared about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're angry at the tech companies but you'd apply to work for them. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. But rent is rent. I'd rather be inside making noise than outside with no money.

S2.say: This is a choice, not the weather; tech companies should pay for it through taxes and workers should have a say.
S2.think: She knows from daily use that routine writing is gone, and there'd be a hundred people for each new AI job.
S2.do: Applies for AI testing and safety jobs despite her anger, moves somewhere cheaper with a flatmate and joins a union or campaign group.
S2.feel: Angry on top, scared about money underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it to people in your field, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be out marching. Shares boom while people lose their jobs? That's the gains going to the people who already own everything. I'd be pushing for a basic income paid for by taxing those profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My career's over in this one. Not just mine, my friends' too. I'd have to start again in something completely different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look seriously at nursing or teaching, something with people in the room. Spend my savings on the training. Organise with other laid-off writers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's gone from under me. But at least I'd be angry with a lot of other people.

S3.say: Shares boom while people lose their jobs; the gains should be taxed to pay for a basic income.
S3.think: Her writing career, and her friends' careers, would be over, and she'd have to start again in something very different.
S3.do: Looks seriously at nursing or teaching, spends her savings on training and organises with other laid-off writers.
S3.feel: Like the ground's gone, but not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it to people in your field, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nobody can say 'just learn a trade'. It's everyone now. I'd say this is the moment to change who owns these machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weirdly, I'd feel less alone. Last time it was people like me. Now it's builders and cooks too, so maybe politics actually has to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for work with people, maybe teaching. And I'd put a lot of time into campaigning, because it'd feel like the only thing that could fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a strange sort of hope that people finally push back together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last time you said your career was over. Does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's still over. It's just that now I wouldn't be the only one telling people it's real.

S4.say: Nobody can say ‘just learn a trade’ now; this is the moment to change who owns the machines.
S4.think: With hands-on workers hit too, she feels less alone and thinks politics might finally have to move.
S4.do: Still aims for teaching or other work with people, and puts a lot of time into campaigning.
S4.feel: Scared, with a strange hope people push back together.
